content: Cystic fibrosis is a complex, multi-system disorder characterized by the production of abnormally thick mucus, which predisposes individuals to recurrent pulmonary infections, often caused by atypical bacterial pathogens. These infections progressively damage the lungs, ultimately leading to respiratory failure and death. Current antibiotic treatments are often ineffective in eradicating bacteria once chronic infection is established, and no new antibiotics with novel mechanisms of action are currently in development. Antibiotic adjuvants, which enhance the effectiveness of antibiotics or the immune system by making bacteria more susceptible, less virulent, or by directly killing them through alternative mechanisms, represent a promising therapeutic avenue. This review updates a previously published analysis on this topic. The objective of this review was to evaluate whether antibiotic adjuvants improve clinical and microbiological outcomes in managing pulmonary infections in individuals with cystic fibrosis. The search strategy included a comprehensive review of the Cystic Fibrosis Trials Register, MEDLINE, and ongoing trial registries, with the most recent searches conducted in early 2020. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-randomized controlled trials comparing antibiotic adjuvant therapies to placebo or no treatment in cystic fibrosis patients. A total of 42 trials were identified, of which eight trials (involving 350 participants) met the inclusion criteria. These trials investigated the effects of β-carotene (one trial, 24 participants), garlic (one trial, 34 participants), KB001-A (a monoclonal antibody; two trials, 196 participants), nitric oxide (two trials, 30 participants), and zinc supplementation (two trials, 66 participants). The zinc trials exclusively involved children, while the other trials included both adults and children. Geographically, three trials were conducted in Europe, one in Asia, and four in the United States. Three interventions—β-carotene, KB001-A, and zinc supplementation—assessed the primary outcome of pulmonary exacerbations. The evidence suggested that β-carotene and KB001-A may have little to no effect on reducing the number of exacerbations (low-quality evidence). Zinc supplementation, based on moderate-quality evidence, likely does not affect the frequency of exacerbations. Respiratory function, measured as forced expiratory volume in one second (FEV1), was evaluated in all included trials. β-carotene and nitric oxide may have little to no impact on FEV1 (low-quality evidence), while garlic likely has no significant effect on FEV1 (moderate-quality evidence). The effects of zinc and KB001-A on FEV1 remain uncertain due to very low-quality evidence. Adverse events were infrequent across all interventions and were generally mild or unrelated to the treatments. In one trial involving 169 participants, KB001-A was compared to placebo for its effect on the time to the next course of antibiotics. The results indicated no significant difference between the two groups (moderate-quality evidence). Quality of life was assessed in the two KB001-A trials, which suggested that KB001-A may have little to no impact on this outcome (low-quality evidence). Sputum microbiology was reported in trials investigating KB001-A and nitric oxide. For KB001-A, there was very low-quality evidence suggesting a numerical reduction in Pseudomonas aeruginosa density, though this was not statistically significant. Nitric oxide trials demonstrated significant reductions in Staphylococcus aureus and near-significant reductions in Pseudomonas aeruginosa, but the quality of this evidence was also very low. In conclusion, no antibiotic adjuvant therapy could be recommended for the treatment of pulmonary infections in cystic fibrosis based on the current evidence. The increasing prevalence of antibiotic-resistant bacteria underscores the limitations of relying solely on antibiotics for managing these infections. There is an urgent need to explore alternative therapeutic strategies, including adjuvant therapies, and further research is essential to develop effective treatment options for this patient population.
